solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: There's no place for mild bitter

indicators.note: saying there is none of something means those letters are taken away from the word

blocks.note: PL is the standard abbreviation for place
placid means calm and gentle

explanation.surface: A drinker complains that the pub has stopped serving mild in favour of bitter, two kinds of British beer.
explanation.walkthrough: Mild and bitter look like a pair of beers; mild is the word losing its PL, and bitter is the definition. Take PL out of PLACID to leave ACID.
explanation.definitionFit: Acid and bitter are both sharp, sour-tasting adjectives, so they are synonyms in taste and in temper.

clue.text: My love wants company in the van

indicators.note: the van is the front, so the company goes ahead of the other part rather than after it

blocks.note: CO is the usual abbreviation for company
love is nil in tennis, the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone's sweetheart would like company while riding in the van.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My love' reads as a pet name, but My stands alone as the exclamation. Coo is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'My!'
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of astonishment, so 'Coo!' and 'My!' are interchangeable interjections.

clue.text: Ambition to succeed? It'll be a long shot

blocks.note: first meaning: determination and energy to achieve
second meaning: a long hit, as off the tee in golf

explanation.surface: A cynic remarks that one's hopes of success are unlikely to come off.
explanation.walkthrough: A long shot sounds like an unlikely chance; here it is literally a long hit, the golfer's opening stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both personal motivation and energy, and a powerful long-distance stroke in golf or cricket.

clue.text: Book with hot photo takes the biscuit

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for book
hot in the sense of lustful
a snap is a quick photograph

explanation.surface: A racy picture book is so outrageous it 'takes the biscuit', a British idiom for being the limit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes the biscuit' is an idiom for being the most outrageous, but here 'the biscuit' is the definition. A brandy snap is a thin rolled ginger biscuit.
explanation.definitionFit: A brandy snap is a crisp lacy ginger wafer, a specific example of a biscuit.

clue.text: Swagger shown by upcoming lawyer with excellent case

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means the letters read from the bottom upwards
a case holds something inside it, so the other part sits within these letters

blocks.note: a DA is a district attorney, an American prosecutor
bravo is a cry of 'excellent!'

explanation.surface: An up-and-coming lawyer struts about with a brilliant case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' looks like the lawyer's brief, but it is the outer word holding the lawyer.
explanation.definitionFit: Bravado is a bold, boastful show of confidence, which is what swagger means as a noun.

clue.text: Where sleepers might be found at every point

blocks.note: first meaning: railway sleepers lie under the length of the track
second meaning: throughout, in every respect

explanation.walkthrough: Sleepers suggests people in bed, but these are the wooden beams under railway rails, and points are also railway switches.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means completely or throughout, and taken literally describes the timber ties laid along a railway track.

clue.text: Small scene in play is Iago's first and last

indicators.note: only the opening and closing letters of the name are kept
one part is placed inside the other

blocks.note: a drama is a play
Iago is the villain of Othello

explanation.surface: In a theatre programme, a short scene in the play belongs to Iago from start to finish.
explanation.walkthrough: The play and Iago suggest Shakespeare, but play just means a drama, and Iago's ends sit inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A diorama is a miniature three-dimensional model of a scene, so a small scene describes it.

clue.text: Can I still cast piece of little substance?

indicators.note: to cast is to throw or mould, so the letters are thrown into a new shape

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A director wonders whether it's still possible to cast actors for a flimsy play.
explanation.walkthrough: Cast and piece suggest a theatre production; a scintilla is a tiny trace.
explanation.definitionFit: A scintilla is a minute amount or trace, a tiny bit with hardly any substance.

clue.text: Babe in a car collecting a new coffee-maker

indicators.note: something new is remade, so these letters are formed into a fresh arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, picked up by the other letters

explanation.surface: A baby in a car seat is fetching a brand new espresso machine.
explanation.walkthrough: A coffee-maker sounds like an appliance; here it is the bean that coffee is made from.
explanation.definitionFit: Arabica beans are the most widely grown coffee seed, so they make coffee in a playful sense.

clue.text: In the past, I got up out of habit

definitions.text: In the past, I got up out of habit

blocks.clueFragment: In the past, I got up out of habit
blocks.note: surface reading: someone long ago rose early from routine
setter's reading: a historical lady mounted a horse with no clothes, a habit being a garment

explanation.walkthrough: Habit means routine on the surface, but it is also clothing (as in a riding habit), and got up means mounted a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend says the Anglo-Saxon noblewoman rode naked through Coventry, so she mounted without any riding habit.

clue.text: King unhappy one Christmas after a turn

indicators.note: turning round makes the letters read back to front

blocks.note: sad means unhappy
I is the Roman numeral for one
Noel is another word for Christmas

explanation.surface: A monarch is miserable one Christmas after taking a turn for the worse.
explanation.walkthrough: Leonidas was the Spartan king who held the pass at Thermopylae.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonidas I was a famous king of ancient Sparta, so he is an example of a king.

clue.text: Vulgar party game for swingers?

blocks.note: base means coarse or low
a ball is a formal dancing party

explanation.surface: A crude party game for wife-swappers is being described.
explanation.walkthrough: Swingers suggests partner-swappers to fit the vulgar party; here they are batters swinging at the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: In baseball the batter swings at each pitch, so its players are literally swingers.

clue.text: A group of dudes close to arrest for desertion

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so just its final letter is used

blocks.note: taken as written
a band is a group of musicians
of and on are interchangeable in phrases like 'think of'
dudes are guys
the final letter of arrest

explanation.surface: A gang of men is about to be arrested for desertion from the army.
explanation.definitionFit: Abandonment and desertion both mean leaving someone or something behind for good, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Get a dry drop of Amarone at home

indicators.note: a drop is a tiny amount, so only the first letter of the wine is taken

blocks.note: taken as written
TT means teetotal, so dry in the sense of not drinking
Amarone is an Italian red wine
in means at home

explanation.surface: Someone fetches a dry Italian red to drink at home.
explanation.walkthrough: Dry looks like a wine description next to Amarone, but it means teetotal.
explanation.definitionFit: To attain is to achieve or reach, which is one sense of get, as in getting a result.

clue.text: Replace heads of old left in African state

indicators.note: the heads of words are their first letters
to replace things is to put them back in a different place, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the opening letters of these three words
taken as written

explanation.surface: Instructions to replace the leaders of a former left-wing government in an African country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'African state' looks like the definition; the state is American, and African is part of the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: California is one of the fifty United States, so it is an example of a state.

clue.text: Out of order train isn't on its way

indicators.note: things out of order are jumbled, so the letters must be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A broken-down train is not going anywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface says the train is stuck; the answer says it is moving.
explanation.definitionFit: In transit describes goods or people travelling between places, which is what being on the way means.

clue.text: Clue guide

blocks.note: first meaning: a hint that helps a detective
second meaning: to show the way

explanation.walkthrough: Two words with nothing between them, each a sense of the same word, pronounced the same way here.
explanation.definitionFit: A lead is a piece of evidence pointing to a solution, and to lead is to go ahead and direct others.

clue.text: Correct turning point for reversing

indicators.note: reversing makes the word run backwards

blocks.note: the turn of the tide is the classic turning point

explanation.surface: A driver corrects their approach by finding the right spot to turn in order to reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a three-point turn; 'the tide has turned' is the idiom behind turning point.
explanation.definitionFit: To edit a text is to correct it, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: It's a little odd and tickles a little

indicators.note: odd means strange or out of the usual form, so the letters are made into a different arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone describes a feeling as slightly strange and mildly ticklish.
explanation.definitionFit: To titillate originally meant to tickle lightly, and now means to excite pleasantly.

clue.text: Piece from editor on touristy city abroad

indicators.note: a piece taken out of a run of words is a stretch of consecutive letters inside them

blocks.note: letters running across the three words

explanation.surface: An editor commissions a travel article about a popular overseas destination.
explanation.definitionFit: Toronto is the largest city in Canada, a city abroad from the British setter's point of view.

clue.text: Large ship must give European a lift by law

indicators.note: lifting a letter in a down entry moves it higher, so it is taken out and put back further up

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for large
a galley is an oared ship

explanation.surface: A big ship is legally required to carry a European passenger.
explanation.walkthrough: L and GALLEY make LGALLEY; the E (European) rises from near the bottom to sit just under the L.
explanation.definitionFit: Legally means according to the law, which is what 'by law' means as an adverb phrase.

clue.text: Not just as brown mops are?

blocks.note: first meaning: not fair or equitable
second meaning, playful: a brown head of hair is not fair, that is not blonde

explanation.walkthrough: Mops means heads of hair; split the answer as UN-FAIR and it describes hair that isn't blonde.
explanation.definitionFit: Unfair means unjust, and fair also means light-coloured hair, so brown hair is literally not fair.

clue.text: Fruit works with, say, grapefruit starter

indicators.note: the starter of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: e.g. means for example
the first letter of grapefruit
a works is a factory, a plant

explanation.surface: Someone suggests a fruit dish that goes well with a grapefruit appetiser.
explanation.walkthrough: Starter looks like a first course next to grapefruit, but it picks out its first letter. Eggplant is the American name for aubergine, botanically a fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: The eggplant is botanically a berry, so the vegetable counts as a fruit.

clue.text: Language seen in loo left by King and Earl

indicators.note: when people have left, they are gone, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: a latrine is a basic toilet
R is short for rex
E is the abbreviation for earl

explanation.surface: Classical graffiti in a toilet was written by a king and an earl.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove R and E from LATRINE. Latin graffiti really survives on Roman latrine walls.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin is the classical tongue of ancient Rome, an example of a language.

clue.text: Man in silk changing foreign capital

indicators.note: things that are changing take a new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: he refers to a man
the letters of in silk rearranged

explanation.surface: A man in a silk outfit is getting changed abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: Changing reads as getting dressed in the silk, but it rearranges those words.
explanation.definitionFit: Helsinki is the capital city of Finland, so it is an example of a capital abroad.

clue.text: Brood on times I left to go to The East

indicators.note: heading the opposite way along the line means the string is read backwards

blocks.note: re means on or concerning
T is short for time, so times gives two of them
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Someone gloomily muses on how often they left for the Orient.
explanation.walkthrough: Brood looks like a verb meaning mope, but it is the noun for a family of young animals. The run made from on, times, I, left reads backwards to give LITTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A litter is a set of young born to one animal at one time, which is a brood.

clue.text: Have seconds in new cafe by the front in Torquay

indicators.note: the seconds of words are their second letters
the front of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: the second letters of these two words
Torquay is a seaside town in Devon

explanation.surface: Diners go back for second helpings in a new seafront café in Torquay.
explanation.walkthrough: Seconds suggests extra helpings of food, which fits the eating theme, but it picks second letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a meal is to eat it, so have and eat are synonyms in this food sense.

clue.text: Writer's stuff is unmoving on radio

indicators.note: what is broadcast on the radio is heard, not seen, so a word that is only pronounced like it is meant

blocks.note: stationary means not moving

explanation.surface: A writer's possessions are stuck in place on a radio programme.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words differ only in an A or an E: stationAry stands still, stationEry is paper and envelopes.
explanation.definitionFit: Stationery is paper, pens and envelopes, the materials a writer uses.

clue.text: Perhaps a school in need of turning around

indicators.note: something turned around faces the other way, so the word reads backwards

blocks.note: Eton is the famous English public school

explanation.surface: A school seems to be badly in need of a turnaround in its fortunes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps a school' looks like it introduces an example of a school; in fact 'Perhaps a' is the definition, because A is a musical note.
explanation.definitionFit: A is one of the musical notes of the scale, so a note is what A perhaps is.
